Great question. In 1968, Garrett Hardin described how people acting in their own interest can deplete a shared resource. Lovett argues that deep professional expertise is a similar shared resource, which he calls the Cognitive Commons.

**How the commons gets depleted**

Organizations used to train new experts as a side effect of needing entry-level workers. Each firm that eliminates an entry-level position keeps all of the efficiency gains, while the cost of lost expertise is spread across the profession.

The paper points to early evidence. Workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations saw a 16% relative drop in employment. Employment for older workers in the same occupations fell by about 8%. Similar worries were raised about calculators in math classrooms in the 1970s.

**Two kinds of expertise**

The paper distinguishes Internalized Mastery, deep knowledge held by individuals, from Distributed Mastery, skill at orchestrating human-AI systems. Since the second depends on the first, a workforce that never builds deep knowledge will struggle to catch subtle AI errors. In one experiment, 80.7% of participants spotted errors in AI recommendations but kept following them.

**What to do about it**

Lovett recommends that governments require every firm to reserve 10% of its jobs for entry-level trainees. He builds on Elinor Ostrom, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009 for her work on governing common resources. Lovett's framework is the most convincing account yet of how AI will affect professional work. The paper concludes that the tragedy is not inevitable but is structurally predictable under current incentives.
